newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FEATURE - Czech human rights campaigners mark anniversary.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Czech human rights campaigners mark anniversary.

text.p: The pony-tails and beards are turning grey and the waistbands are wider but the dissident intellectuals who launched one of Eastern Europe's first human rights groups still know how to party.
In the Baroque splendour of Prague Castle's Spanish Hall, signatories of the Charter 77 declaration commemorated its 20th anniversary with speeches, free beer, and rock-and-roll.

There was one notable absentee -- Charter 77's co-founder and now Czech President Vaclav Havel. The dissident playwright who spent five years in Czechoslovak jails for his political views is recovering from surgery for lung cancer.
But his recorded greeting caught the irony of the moment.

"Who of those who were in at the birth of Charter 77 or, knowing fully what they could expect, signed it later, could have imagined they would commemorate their action in the Spanish Hall of Prague Castle as citizens of a free state?" Havel said. His words were loudly cheered.
Charter 77 was founded in January 1977, eight years after the 1968 Warsaw Pact intervention to crush the liberalisation, led by Alexander Dubcek, known as the "Prague Spring".

"The spine of the national spirit was broken, not in 1968 but a year later when Dubcek and his friends resigned...and (communist leader Gustav) Husak and his people came," said Peter Pithart, a Charter signatory who now heads the upper house of parliament.
The movement grew out of a manifesto accusing the hardline communist authorities of violating human rights and international commitments. The first signatories were 242 dissidents, including Havel.
Eventually, more than 2,000 people signed the charter.
SECRET POLICE HARASSMENT
Those who signed were constantly harassed by secret police, many lost their jobs and were forced to make a living cleaning windows or stoking central heating boilers.
Havel hauled beer kegs at a brewery.

Many went to prison. Havel was jailed in 1979 and has said he dreamed in his cell of the day when Charter signatories could meet, along with Jiri Dienstbier who was later to become foreign minister from 1990 to 1992.

"It was very important for Czech political culture," said Dienstbier, today the leader of a small centrist grouping. "These people are in different parties now...but it was like a school for democracy."

Charter 77 played a leading role in the bloodless 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which overthrew the communists. Havel became president and many of the dissident band achieved high political and other office.

Since then Czechoslovakia has been through the 1993 Velvet Divorce between the Czech and Slovak republics and the Czechs have faced the sobering reality of monetarist Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's pro-market economic reforms.
But at the 20th birthday party, held earlier this month, even the bad old days were remembered with a smile.
Guests were watched over by groups of policemen in drab green uniforms and drumming their gloved hands with truncheons.
For a moment, until it dawned that their gun holsters were empty, it could have been 1977.
Among those "questioned", were Interior Minister Jan Ruml, a former dissident who was denied a college education and still sports a rat's tail haircut.
ONCE-BANNED GROUP ROCKS INTO THE PAST

The atmosphere was charged as Jaroslav Hutka, one of Czechoslovakia's most popular singers in the 1970s, took the stage. Like many artists, he was exiled by the communists and only returned in the regime's death throes in late 1989.
But the hall, normally reserved for stiff banquets for visiting heads of state, really started to rock when the underground band Plastic People of the Universe began to play.
The band's banning and the prosecution of some of its members for a breach of the peace in the 1970s was one of the sparks for the Charter movement.
As the Plastic People played some of their old psychedelic classics, the audience, including Interior Minister Ruml were dancing in front of the stage.
"No matter where we all are today, having different political opinions, the basic idea of solidarity and the fight against totalitarianism remains," he said.
In November 1992, Charter leaders wound up the movement, insisting it had done its job.

But Prague's ancient Charles University marked the 20th anniversary by awarding an honorary doctorate to Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi for her "active participation in the fight for democracy, freedom and human rights".
